direct.title: Pizza Dough Calculator – yeast from time & temperature
direct.description: Free pizza dough calculator: flour, water, salt and yeast in grams, with the yeast worked out from your fermentation time and temperature. Neapolitan, New York and Roman presets, cold fermentation, metric and imperial.
direct.heading: Pizza Dough Calculator
direct.guideTitle: How the pizza dough calculator works
direct.intro: Most dough recipes fix the amount of yeast and leave you to fit your day around it. This calculator works the other way round: you say how long the dough has and how warm it will be, and it works out the yeast that makes the dough ready on time. Everything else follows from the number of pizzas, the weight of each dough ball and the dough's baker's percentages.

direct.tableIntro: Yeast as a percentage of the flour weight for common schedules, worked out by this calculator for a batch of four Neapolitan dough balls.

poolish.title: Poolish Pizza Dough Calculator – poolish yeast by time
poolish.description: Calculate poolish pizza dough: flour, water and yeast for the poolish and the final dough in grams, with the yeast worked out from how long and how warm the poolish ripens. Free, metric and imperial.
poolish.heading: Poolish Pizza Calculator
poolish.intro: A poolish is a preferment of equal parts flour and water with a pinch of yeast, left to ripen for several hours before the dough is mixed. This calculator splits the recipe into the poolish and the final dough, sets the poolish yeast so it peaks when you need it, and adds only as much yeast to the final dough as its own schedule still needs.

sections.heading: What a poolish does
paragraphs: During its long, wet ripening the poolish builds aroma and enzymes that gently break down starch and gluten. The result is a dough that stretches easily, a light, open crust and a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavour — without the sourness of a sourdough.
For pizza, 25–35 % of the flour in the poolish is typical. More gives a stronger flavour and a more extensible dough, and the final dough then needs less yeast, or none at all.

sections.heading: When the poolish is ripe
paragraphs: A ripe poolish has doubled or tripled, is full of bubbles and smells fruity and slightly sweet. Use it when the dome is just starting to flatten. Once it has collapsed and smells sharply sour or of alcohol, it has gone too far.

The amount of yeast decides when that point comes: the longer and cooler, the less yeast. A 16-hour poolish needs only a fraction of the yeast of a 4-hour one. If your plans change, a ripe poolish keeps in the fridge for up to about a day.

faq.question: How much poolish should pizza dough have?
faq.answer: Usually 25–35 % of the total flour; this calculator starts at 30 %. Up to 50 % gives a stronger flavour and an even more extensible dough.

faq.question: Does poolish pizza dough need extra yeast?
faq.answer: Often only a little. The ripe poolish already brings plenty of active yeast, so the calculator adds only what the final dough's own schedule still needs — and none at all if the poolish alone is enough.

faq.question: Can a poolish go in the fridge?
faq.answer: A poolish ripens best in the warmth, so let it ripen at room temperature first. A ripe poolish then keeps in the fridge for up to about 24 hours; let it warm up for 30–60 minutes before mixing it into the dough.

poolish.tableHeading: How much yeast for a poolish?
poolish.tableIntro: Yeast as a percentage of the flour in the poolish, for a poolish that ripens in the given time, worked out by this calculator.

biga.title: Biga Pizza Dough Calculator – biga yeast & timings
biga.description: Calculate biga pizza dough: flour, water and yeast for the biga and the final dough in grams, with the biga yeast worked out from its time and temperature. From 20 to 100 % biga, metric and imperial.
biga.heading: Biga Pizza Calculator
biga.intro: A biga is a stiff Italian preferment: flour with only about 45 % water and a little yeast, mixed into a crumbly mass and left to ripen for around 16–18 hours. This calculator splits the recipe into the biga and the final dough, sets the biga yeast for your time and temperature, and works out how much yeast, if any, the final dough still needs.

sections.heading: What a biga does
paragraphs: With so little water the yeast works slowly, and the biga develops a gentle, slightly alcoholic and fruity aroma rather than acidity. It strengthens the gluten, so biga doughs take high hydration well and bake into a crisp, airy crust with a very open crumb.
Pizzerias put anything from 20 to 100 % of the flour into the biga. At 50 % and more the biga brings so much mature yeast that the final dough usually needs no extra yeast and only a short rise.

sections.heading: Mixing and ripening a biga
paragraphs: Dissolve the yeast in cool water, add the flour and mix only briefly, until the water is absorbed and the biga looks like coarse, moist crumbs. Do not knead it into a smooth ball. The classic biga ripens for 16–18 hours at 16–18 °C with about 1 % fresh yeast, mixed to around 20 °C.

A ripe biga has grown by only about a fifth, the crumbs look puffy, and it smells gently of alcohol and fruit. If it has doubled or smells sharp, it has gone too far. Tear it into small pieces before it goes into the final dough, or it will not mix in evenly.

faq.question: How much biga should pizza dough have?
faq.answer: Anything from 20 to 100 % of the flour. 30–50 % is a good start, and this calculator opens at 50 %. The more biga, the more flavour and strength — and the less yeast and time the final dough needs.

faq.question: What hydration should a biga have?
faq.answer: The classic biga uses 44–45 % water. Up to about 55–60 % is easier to mix by hand and ferments a little faster. The rest of the recipe's water goes into the final dough.

faq.question: Does a biga dough need extra yeast?
faq.answer: At 50 % biga or more, usually not: the ripe biga carries enough yeast for a short final rise. With less biga or a long cold phase, the calculator adds the little the final dough still needs.

biga.tableHeading: How much yeast for a biga?
biga.tableIntro: Yeast as a percentage of the flour in the biga, for a biga that ripens in the given time, worked out by this calculator.

sourdough.title: Sourdough Pizza Dough Calculator – starter amount & feeding
sourdough.description: Calculate sourdough pizza dough: how much starter for your fermentation time and temperature, when and how to feed it, and the flour, water and salt in grams. No commercial yeast, with cold fermentation.
sourdough.heading: Sourdough Pizza Calculator
sourdough.intro: A sourdough pizza is leavened by a starter instead of commercial yeast. This calculator works out how much ripe starter your schedule needs, tells you when and in what ratio to feed it so it peaks just as you mix, and takes its flour and water off the final dough so the hydration stays exactly as set.

sections.heading: How much starter?
paragraphs: The more starter, the faster the dough. For pizza that rests 1–3 days in the fridge, 10–25 % of the flour weight is typical; a dough that ferments for a whole day at room temperature needs only 3–5 %, and a same-day dough 25 % or more in a warm spot.

The calculator takes the figure from the same fermentation model as the yeast doughs, so time, temperature and the fridge all count the same way. Sourdough varies more than yeast, though — a sluggish starter or a cool kitchen can add hours.

sections.heading: Feeding the starter
paragraphs: Use the starter at its peak: doubled or more, domed, full of bubbles and pleasantly sour. The feeding ratio sets when that happens — at 22 °C a 1:1:1 feed peaks after about 6 hours, 1:2:2 after about 9 and 1:4:4 after about 12.
The warmer, the faster: every 6 °C roughly halves the time. The calculator picks the ratio from how long before mixing you feed it, and builds a little extra for you to keep.

faq.question: How much starter goes into sourdough pizza dough?
faq.answer: Typically 10–25 % of the flour weight for a dough with a fridge phase, and 3–5 % for 24 hours at room temperature. The calculator works it out from your schedule — with the defaults (24 hours in the fridge) it comes to about 22 %.

faq.question: Can I use a stiff starter (lievito madre)?
faq.answer: Yes. Set the starter hydration to around 50 %. Its flour and water are counted in the recipe either way, so the dough keeps exactly the hydration you set.

faq.question: Does sourdough pizza need extra yeast?
faq.answer: No. An active starter leavens the dough on its own, and this calculator adds no commercial yeast. If your starter is sluggish, give the dough more time rather than adding yeast.

sourdough.tableHeading: How much starter for pizza dough?
sourdough.tableIntro: Ripe starter at 100 % hydration, as a percentage of the flour weight, for common schedules — worked out by this calculator.

direct.hint: All the yeast goes into one dough. The simplest method — the flavour comes from the fermentation schedule alone.

room.label: At room temperature
room.hint: The classic poolish: it ripens in the warmth over about 12 hours and is used at its peak — domed, bubbly, just starting to settle.

fridge.label: Overnight in the fridge
fridge.hint: An hour at room temperature to get the yeast going, then about 16 hours in the fridge. It ripens slowly and holds its peak longer, which makes it easy to fit around a working day — at the cost of noticeably more yeast.

biga.label: Biga
biga.hint: Part or all of the flour ferments first as a stiff, crumbly preferment with about 45 % water, typically 16–18 hours. Builds strength for an airy, crisp crust and a mild, slightly fruity aroma.
biga.shareTooltip: How much of the recipe's total flour goes into the biga. Anything from 20 to 100 % is used; 30–50 % is a good start. The more biga, the shorter the final dough's rise.
biga.hydrationTooltip: Water in the biga, as a percentage of its own flour. The classic biga uses 44–45 %; up to about 60 % is easier to mix by hand.
biga.timeTooltip: Hours at room temperature — 0 for a biga that only goes in the fridge. The yeast is worked out for the whole schedule.
biga.yeastNote: Biga yeast: {{percent}} % {{yeast}} relative to the biga flour.
biga.noExtraYeast: No extra yeast in the final dough — the ripe biga leavens it on its own.
biga.surplus: The biga alone brings more leavening than this schedule needs, so no yeast goes into the final dough — and the dough will still be ready early, after about {{hours}} h at room temperature instead of {{planned}} h. Shorten the room-temperature time or use less biga.
biga.surplusTooShort: The biga alone brings more leavening than even the shortest schedule needs, so the dough will be ready early. Use less biga or add a longer cold phase.
biga.knead: Mix the dough: tear the biga into small pieces and mix it with most of the water{{yeast}} until it starts to come together. Add the flour, then the salt, and work in the remaining water and the ice a little at a time. Knead until the dough is smooth and elastic.
biga.stepIntro: Biga, {{hours}} h before you mix the dough:
biga.mix: dissolve {{yeast}} yeast in {{water}} water{{waterTemp}}, add {{flour}} flour and mix only until the water is absorbed — a shaggy mass of moist crumbs, not a smooth dough.
biga.ripe: It is ripe when it has grown slightly, looks puffy and smells gently of alcohol and fruit.

classic.label: Classic (Giorilli)
classic.hint: The standard Italian biga: 44–45 % water and about 1 % fresh yeast, ripened for 16–18 hours somewhere cool, ideally 16–18 °C.

cold.label: Cold biga (biga fredda)
cold.hint: Mixed warm, to about 25 °C, with 50 % water, then straight into the fridge for 24–48 hours. Forgiving of a warm kitchen, with a milder, more controlled aroma.

long.label: Long biga (48 h)
long.hint: 24 hours in the fridge, then 24 hours at 18–20 °C, with 40–42 % water and very little yeast — a 48-hour biga for the most aroma. With a 24-hour final dough it makes a 72-hour pizza.

sourdough.label: Sourdough
sourdough.hint: No commercial yeast: an active sourdough starter leavens the dough. Gives a deeper, gently tangy flavour and a crisp, blistered crust — and the amount of starter follows from your schedule.
sourdough.step: Feed the starter {{hours}} h before you mix the dough: stir {{seed}} ripe starter with {{flour}} flour and {{water}} water, cover and leave at {{temp}}. It is ready when it has at least doubled, is domed and full of bubbles — use it at its peak.
sourdough.knead: Mix the dough: dissolve the starter in the water and the ice, add the flour and mix until no dry flour is left, then work in the salt. Knead for 10–15 minutes until the dough is smooth and elastic.

pizzaStyleHints.newyork: Slightly drier dough with oil and sugar, long cold fermentation, crisp base.
pizzaStyleHints.roman: Very wet dough for thin, crunchy pizza — usually baked in a tray or on a stone.

starter.heading: Sourdough starter
starter.percentTooltip: Ripe starter as a percentage of the total flour weight. 15–25 % is typical for pizza fermented in the fridge; 3–5 % for 24 hours at room temperature.
starter.hydrationTooltip: Water in the starter as a percentage of its flour: 100 % for a liquid starter, around 50 % for a stiff one (lievito madre). Its flour and water count towards the recipe's totals.

fermentation.roomTimeTooltip: Total time at room temperature, split over the bulk rise and the final proof. At least {{minimum}} h are needed.
fermentation.coldTimeTooltip: Time in the fridge between the bulk rise and balling. Set 0 to skip the cold fermentation.

split.label: Split of the room-temperature time
split.tooltip: Where the room-temperature hours go: rising as one piece before the fridge, or proving as balls after it. Longer bulk builds flavour and gluten; longer final proof gives lighter balls that are easier to stretch.
split.noSlack: Raise the room-temperature time above {{minimum}} h to shift hours between the two phases.

fresh.label: Fresh yeast (cake yeast)
fresh.hint: The moist block from the fridge. Crumble it straight into the dough or dissolve it in part of the water. This is the reference amount all other types are converted from.

instant.label: Instant dry yeast
instant.hint: Fine granules that are stirred straight into the flour — no soaking needed. You need about 40 % of the fresh-yeast amount.

active.label: Active dry yeast (needs rehydrating)
active.hint: Coarser granules that must first be woken up: stir into lukewarm water (about {{temp}}) with a pinch of sugar and wait 10 minutes until it foams, then add it to the dough. You need about 50 % of the fresh-yeast amount.

calculator.yeastPercentTooltip: Percentage of the flour weight, for the yeast type selected above.
calculator.yeastPercentFinalTooltip: Yeast added to the final dough, as a percentage of the total flour. At 0 the preferment does all the leavening.
calculator.oilPercentTooltip: Percentage of the flour weight (0 = no oil). Makes the base softer and browner.
calculator.sugarPercentTooltip: Percentage of the flour weight (0 = no sugar). Helps the crust colour in a home oven.

afterCold.label: After the cold fermentation
afterCold.hint: The whole batch goes into the fridge as one mass and is divided when it comes out. The mass cools slowly, so it keeps fermenting for hours on the way down — less yeast is needed.

beforeCold.label: Before the cold fermentation
beforeCold.hint: The dough is divided and balled before it goes into the fridge. Balls chill much faster than a single mass, so they bank less fermentation while cooling — slightly more yeast is needed. Easier to store, and the balls are ready to use straight from the fridge.

thermalModel.label: Account for the dough cooling down
thermalModel.onHint: The fridge phase is weighted by how long the dough actually takes to get cold, which depends on the batch size and on whether it is retarded in bulk or as balls.
thermalModel.offHint: The original estimate: the fridge phase counts as plain wall-clock hours, whatever the size or shape of the dough.

sections.heading: Baker's percentages
paragraphs: Every ingredient is given as a percentage of the flour weight, with the flour itself at 100 %. A Neapolitan dough at 65 % hydration and 2.5 % salt uses 650 g of water and 25 g of salt for each kilogram of flour.

To get from there to grams, the calculator adds up all the percentages and divides the total dough weight — pizzas × ball weight — by that sum. That gives the flour, and every other ingredient is the flour times its percentage.

sections.heading: Yeast from time and temperature
paragraphs: Yeast works faster the warmer it is and the longer it has, so the same dough can need ten times more yeast for a same-day bake than for a three-day cold ferment. The calculator models the room-temperature hours and the fridge hours separately and combines them, so any mix of the two gives a sensible amount.
Fresh, instant and active dry yeast are converted automatically: instant dry yeast is about 40 % of the fresh-yeast weight, active dry yeast about 50 %.

sections.heading: Cold fermentation in the fridge
paragraphs: A long, cold rest builds flavour and makes the dough easier to stretch, without it over-proving. The fridge does not stop fermentation though: the dough takes hours to cool down, and it keeps working while it does.

How long depends on its size. A whole batch retarded in one piece cools much more slowly than the same dough divided into balls, so it banks more fermentation on the way down and needs a little less yeast. The calculator accounts for this when it is switched on.

items.question: How long should pizza dough ferment?
items.answer: A same-day dough needs at least 5 hours at room temperature. Most pizzerias ferment for 24 to 72 hours with most of that time in the fridge, which gives more flavour and a dough that is easier to stretch. Choose the schedule that fits your day, and the calculator sets the yeast to match.

items.question: What hydration should pizza dough have?
items.answer: Neapolitan dough is usually around 60–65 % water, New York style around 60–63 % with a little oil and sugar, and Roman-style pizza 70–80 %. Higher hydration gives a lighter, more open crust but is stickier to handle.

items.question: How do I convert fresh yeast to dry yeast?
items.answer: Use about 40 % of the fresh-yeast weight for instant dry yeast and about 50 % for active dry yeast. 10 g of fresh yeast becomes about 4 g instant or 5 g active dry. Pick the yeast type in the calculator and it converts for you.

items.question: Should the dough go into the fridge in one piece or as balls?
items.answer: Both work. In one piece the dough cools slowly and keeps fermenting for hours on the way down, so it needs slightly less yeast and is shaped after the fridge. As balls it chills faster, needs slightly more yeast, and can go straight from the fridge to the final proof.

items.question: Why add ice to pizza dough?
items.answer: Kneading warms the dough, and warm dough ferments faster than planned. Weighing part of the water as ice keeps it cool. The ice is not extra water — the hydration stays the same — and about 10 % of the water is enough for hand kneading.

footer.privacy: No cookies, no tracking, no analytics, and no external fonts or scripts. The calculator runs entirely in your browser — nothing you enter is ever sent to a server. Your settings live in the page address after the “#”, which browsers never send to a server, so a recipe link only shares them with whoever you give it to; the calendar file and the PDF are made in your browser too. The only thing kept is your chosen language and unit system, saved in this browser so the page remembers them; clearing your site data removes them again.
